reasons_add: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Solomon wrote the letter after postponing judgment on the hoopoe.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Solomon withheld judgment until he could distinguish the hoopoe's truth from falsehood, then wrote the letter.

Al-Zajjāj lists five forms and calls retention of yāʾ the commonest and strongest; he derives the form from فألقيه, explaining that the yāʾ deleted by the jussive may disappear before the pronoun hāʾ.
Al-Zajjāj includes the form with yāʾ dropped and kasra retained; he relates it to the preference for dropping yāʾ after hāʾ in ألقيه.
Al-Zajjāj includes a still hāʾ among the five reported forms.
Al-Zajjāj says the wāw form restores the original connected pronoun ending, as in ألقيتهو; at a pause or in writing it is represented by hāʾ.
Al-Zajjāj likens dropping wāw while retaining ḍamma to dropping yāʾ while retaining kasra.
Al-Zajjāj distinguishes the verb's jussive deletion of yāʾ from its object pronoun: the pronoun itself is not jussive, so he calls a still hāʾ reading mistaken.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Wahb's account that the hoopoe stayed close enough to observe the rulers' reply.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Ibn Zayd's reading of tawallā as returning to Solomon after delivering the letter.
Wahb, as reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya, has the hoopoe withdraw yet remain near enough to observe the reply.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Ibn Zayd's explicit ordering: observation is logically before withdrawal.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Wahb's description of the withdrawal as courtly etiquette while the bird stays within hearing.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya links the letter to Solomon's postponed judgment until the hoopoe's truth or falsehood could be determined.
Al-Zajjāj refers readers to his fuller explanation of the same pronoun construction at 4:75.
